feedback: If a child counts the start number as the first step (8+3 → '8,9,10' = 10), point out that 8 is where you START, and the first hop lands on 9 — count the landings, not the starting spot.
If a child starts at 1 and counts everything, gently cover the first group, say '8', and count on from there; this earlier stage matures with number sense, so model rather than drill.
For subtraction going the wrong way, link counting back to 'one less each time' and track the backward hops with fingers.
If a child always starts from the first-written number (2 for 2+9), ask which number gives fewer hops and why starting at 9 is quicker.
activities.intendedInsight: Starting AT the larger number and taking just a few hops lands on the same answer as counting everything from one, but is faster; the first count is the next number along from the start (9 for 8+3; 11 when counting back from 12 for 12−3), not the start number.
learnerActions: On a number line or number track, set the start at the larger number (8 for 8+3) and make three hops forward, saying the number you LAND on each time: '9, 10, 11' — not '8'.
Keep track of how many hops you have made using fingers or marks, so you take exactly three.
Switch to count-back mode for 12−3: start at 12 and hop backward three times, saying '11, 10, 9'.
For 2+9, decide which number to start from and explain why you start at 9, not 2.
Narrate out loud where you start and how many steps you take.
If it helps, show the same forward hops on a bead string; a hundred square can be used later to extend counting on and back to larger numbers.
activities.title: Hop along the number line: count on and count back

feedback: Watch for an off-by-one answer (10 for 8+3): the result is 11 — recount the landings, not the start.
If the chosen start for 2+9 is 2, note that starting at 9 means only two hops instead of nine.
For 6+2, start at 6 and count on '7, 8' — two hops lands on 8.
activities.intendedInsight: Repeated, varied practice consolidates counting on from the larger addend and counting back accurately, reinforcing where the count begins.
learnerActions: Draw the jumps on a number line for 8+3 and for 12−3, labelling each landing number.
Answer: 'Which number should you start counting from for 2+9?' and justify the choice.
Fill in results for several count-on and count-back sums (for example 6+2), checking you did not count the start as a step.
activities.title: Spaced practice: draw the hops and choose the start

feedback: If the explanation defends counting all from one, model covering the first group and counting on, and ask which took fewer counts.
Praise explanations that connect counting on to adding and counting back to 'one less each time'.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating why you start from the larger number and that counting on is adding surfaces (and helps move past) a counting-all habit.
learnerActions: Work out a sum and narrate where you start and how many steps you take.
Answer questions like 'Why did you start at 8 and not at 1?' and 'Which is quicker for 8+3 — counting everything or counting on? Why?'.
Explain in your own words how counting on is a way of adding.
activities.title: Talk it through: why start at the bigger number?
